title: The Power-of-Two Predicate
content: `IsPowTwo d` says `d = 2 ^ k` for some `k : ℕ`. The basic instances `isPowTwo_one`, `isPowTwo_two`, `isPowTwo_pow` record that 1, 2, and every 2^k satisfy it. This single ℕ-level predicate is reused on both sides of the constructibility story: it is applied to a polynomial's degree (Wantzel) and to a finite group's order (Galois).
mathContext: Wantzel's criterion states an algebraic number $\alpha$ is constructible only if $[\mathbb{Q}(\alpha):\mathbb{Q}] = 2^k$. The Galois refinement asks that $|\mathrm{Gal}|=2^k$. Both are instances of $d \in \{2^k : k \in \mathbb{N}\}$.

title: The Core Obstruction: One Odd Prime Factor Suffices
content: `not_isPowTwo_of_odd_prime_dvd`: if an odd prime `q` divides `d`, then `d` is not a power of two. The proof is three steps and no case analysis: assume `d = 2^k`; then `q ∣ 2^k` gives `q ∣ 2` by `Nat.Prime.dvd_of_dvd_pow`; then `q = 2` by `Nat.prime_dvd_prime_iff_eq`, contradicting `q ≠ 2`. This is the entire arithmetic content of every classical compass-and-straightedge impossibility.
mathContext: If $d = 2^k$ then the only prime dividing $d$ is 2. Contrapositively, any odd prime divisor is an obstruction. For $d = 3$ (the degree of $\cos 20°$, $\sqrt[3]{2}$, $\cos 2\pi/7$) the odd prime is 3 itself.
prerequisites: a prime dividing a^n divides a
p ∣ q ↔ p = q for primes

title: Full Characterization of Powers of Two
content: `isPowTwo_iff_unique_prime_two`: for `d ≠ 0`, `IsPowTwo d ↔ (every prime factor of d is 2)`. The forward direction reuses the core obstruction's first half; the converse invokes `Nat.eq_prime_pow_of_unique_prime_dvd`, which reconstructs `d = 2 ^ (length of d.primeFactorsList)` when 2 is the sole prime factor.
mathContext: By unique factorization, $d = \prod p_i^{e_i}$; $d$ is a power of two iff that product has only the prime 2, i.e. $d = 2^{\Omega(d)}$ where $\Omega$ counts prime factors with multiplicity.

title: Odd Numbers Above One, and the Concrete Degrees 3, 5, 6
content: `not_isPowTwo_of_odd_gt_one` shows any odd `d > 1` is non-power-of-two: extract a prime factor via `Nat.exists_prime_and_dvd`, prove it is odd (and hence ≠ 2) by `omega` on the parities, then apply the core obstruction. The concrete instances `not_isPowTwo_three`, `not_isPowTwo_five`, `not_isPowTwo_six` (the last using the odd prime 3 ∣ 6) are the values the polynomial applications consume.
mathContext: Degree 3 governs trisection, cube doubling, and the 7-gon; degree 5 governs the regular 11-gon; degree 6 = 2·3 shows the criterion catches even numbers with an odd factor (e.g. cos 2π/13).
prerequisites: every n ≠ 1 has a prime factor

title: Wantzel Degree Side: One Proof for Three Classical Impossibilities
content: `DegreePowerOfTwo p` is `IsPowTwo p.natDegree`. `not_degreePowerOfTwo_of_natDegree_three` then closes angle trisection (cos 20°), cube doubling (∛2), and the regular 7-gon (cos 2π/7) in one line, since all three minimal polynomials have degree 3. `not_degreePowerOfTwo_of_natDegree_five` adds a case the parent does not have — the regular 11-gon, whose cos(2π/11) has a degree-5 minimal polynomial — and `not_degreePowerOfTwo_of_odd_prime_dvd` / `_of_odd_degree` give the general statements.
mathContext: Wantzel: $\alpha$ constructible $\Rightarrow [\mathbb{Q}(\alpha):\mathbb{Q}] = \deg(\mathrm{minpoly}\,\alpha) = 2^k$. A degree with an odd prime factor therefore certifies non-constructibility.

title: Galois Group Side: The Same Lemma, Mirrored
content: `IsTwoGroup G` is `IsPowTwo (Fintype.card G)`. `not_isTwoGroup_of_odd_prime_dvd` is literally `not_isPowTwo_of_odd_prime_dvd` applied to the group order, and `isTwoGroup_iff_isPowTwo_card` records that the degree predicate and the group predicate share one arithmetic core. `exists_orderOf_eq_of_prime_dvd_card` packages Cauchy's theorem (`exists_prime_orderOf_dvd_card`) to exhibit a concrete element of the offending odd-prime order — a witness that cannot live in a 2-group.
mathContext: The Wantzel–Galois characterization makes constructibility equivalent to $\mathrm{Gal}(\mathrm{minpoly}\,\alpha)$ being a 2-group. An odd prime $q \mid |\mathrm{Gal}|$ obstructs this, and Cauchy's theorem produces an order-$q$ element realizing the obstruction.
